_comment: World-literature shard source — Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), fetched 2026-07-25. Authored because the existing lit shard carries an English-department canon (Homer, Shakespeare, Austen, Dickens) while world-literature courses teach traditions and modes across languages: the hit rate for world-lit was 1/14. Concepts here are tradition- and mode-level, not work-level. Source snapshots are faithful condensations built around sentences quoted verbatim from the cited articles.

sourceSnapshots.wikipedia:world-literature: World literature is used to refer to the world's total national literature and the circulation of works into the wider world beyond their country of origin. A work enters into world literature by a double process: first, by being read as literature; second, by circulating out into a broader world beyond its linguistic and cultural point of origin. The intellectual creations of individual nations become common property. Works that thrive as world literature are ones that work well and even gain meaning through translation. Casanova explores the ways in which the works of peripheral writers must circulate into metropolitan centers in order to achieve recognition as being world literature.
sourceSnapshots.wikipedia:frame-story: A frame story, also known as a frame tale, framing device, or frame narrative, is a literary technique that serves as a companion piece to a story within a story. The frame story leads readers from a first story into one or more other stories within it. The frame story may also be used to inform readers about aspects of the secondary narratives that may otherwise be hard to understand. A frame story is a literary device that acts as a convenient conceit to organize a set of smaller narratives. A typical frame story is One Thousand and One Nights, in which the character Scheherazade narrates a set of fairy tales to the Sultan. To be a frame narrative, the story must act primarily as an occasion for the telling of other stories.
sourceSnapshots.wikipedia:magic-realism: Magic realism presents magical or supernatural phenomena presented in an otherwise real-world or mundane setting. Magical events are presented as ordinary occurrences; therefore, the reader accepts the marvelous as normal and common. What may seem extraordinary or even uncanny is considered ordinary for the characters themselves. The narrator is indifferent, a characteristic enhanced by this absence of explanation of fantastic events. In magic realism the supernatural realm blends with the natural, familiar world, arriving at the combination of two layers of reality. Magical realism uses a substantial amount of realistic detail and employs magical elements to make a point about reality.
sourceSnapshots.wikipedia:postcolonial-literature: Postcolonial literature is the literature by people from formerly colonized countries. Postcolonial literature often addresses the problems and consequences of the colonization and subsequent decolonization of a country. It addresses the role of literature in perpetuating and challenging what postcolonial critic Edward Said refers to as cultural imperialism. Pramod Nayar defines postcolonial literature as that which negotiates with, contests, and subverts Euro-American ideologies and representations. Postcolonial literary theory re-examines colonial and postcolonial literature, especially concentrating upon the social discourse between the colonizer and the colonized. Language and literature were factors in consolidating this sense of national identity to resist the impact of colonialism.

definition.text: World literature is the body of works that circulate beyond their country of origin and are read as literature in a wider world.

anchor.quote: circulation of works into the wider world beyond their country of origin

facts.text: A work enters world literature by being read as literature and by circulating beyond its origin.

anchor.quote: A work enters into world literature by a double process

facts.text: Works that thrive as world literature often gain meaning through translation rather than losing it.

anchor.quote: Works that thrive as world literature are ones that work well and even gain meaning through translation

facts.text: Peripheral writers must circulate into metropolitan centres to be recognised as world literature.

anchor.quote: must circulate into metropolitan centers in order to achieve recognition

misconceptions.text: Students assume world literature simply means any book written outside their own country.
misconceptions.corrective: Origin is not the criterion: a work counts once it circulates and is read beyond its linguistic home, which is why circulation and translation do the defining work.

examples.text: A novel widely read only in its country of publication is national literature; once translated and taught abroad it enters world literature.

mcBank.stem: A celebrated novel is read only within its country of publication and has never been translated. On the circulation criterion it is best described as
options: national literature until it circulates abroad
world literature by virtue of its quality
untranslatable by definition
a frame narrative

definition.text: A frame narrative is an outer story whose main purpose is to occasion the telling of other stories inside it.

anchor.quote: a literary technique that serves as a companion piece to a story within a story

facts.text: The frame leads readers from a first story into one or more stories contained within it.

anchor.quote: The frame story leads readers from a first story into one or more other stories within it

facts.text: The outer story can supply context that would make the inner narratives hard to follow.

anchor.quote: inform readers about aspects of the secondary narratives that may otherwise be hard to understand

facts.text: One Thousand and One Nights is the standard example, with Scheherazade narrating to the Sultan.

anchor.quote: A typical frame story is One Thousand and One Nights

misconceptions.text: Students treat any story that contains a flashback or anecdote as a frame narrative.
misconceptions.corrective: The test is function, not presence: the outer story must exist primarily so the inner stories can be told, rather than merely containing one.

examples.text: In One Thousand and One Nights the Sultan's threat is what makes each night's tale necessary, so the outer story exists to occasion the inner ones.

mcBank.stem: A novel opens with a character recalling one childhood anecdote before proceeding with its own plot. On the functional test this is
options: not a frame narrative, since the outer story is the main story
a frame narrative because a story is contained
a frame narrative only if the anecdote is long
world literature by circulation

definition.text: Magic realism places supernatural events inside an ordinary, realistically detailed world and treats them as unremarkable.

anchor.quote: magical or supernatural phenomena presented in an otherwise real-world or mundane setting

facts.text: Magical events are presented as ordinary, so the reader accepts the marvellous as normal.

anchor.quote: Magical events are presented as ordinary occurrences

facts.text: The narrator stays indifferent and offers no explanation for the fantastic event.

anchor.quote: The narrator is indifferent, a characteristic enhanced by this absence of explanation

facts.text: Substantial realistic detail carries the magical element toward a point about reality.

anchor.quote: uses a substantial amount of realistic detail and employs magical elements to make a point about reality

misconceptions.text: Students classify any story containing magic as magic realism.
misconceptions.corrective: The distinguishing move is the narrator's indifference: in fantasy the marvellous is remarked upon and explained, while here it passes without comment inside a realistic world.

examples.text: A character sprouting wings is met by neighbours discussing what to feed him, and the narration never pauses to justify the wings.

mcBank.stem: In a realistic village setting a character levitates and the narrator neither explains nor remarks on it. This handling is characteristic of
options: magic realism, given the indifferent narration
high fantasy world-building
a frame narrative device
postcolonial critique

definition.text: Postcolonial literature is writing from formerly colonised societies that engages the consequences of colonisation and decolonisation.

anchor.quote: Postcolonial literature is the literature by people from formerly colonized countries

facts.text: It addresses the problems and consequences of colonisation and of subsequent decolonisation.

anchor.quote: addresses the problems and consequences of the colonization and subsequent decolonization

facts.text: It both perpetuates and challenges what Said termed cultural imperialism.

anchor.quote: perpetuating and challenging what postcolonial critic Edward Said refers to as cultural imperialism

facts.text: Nayar defines it as writing that negotiates with, contests and subverts Euro-American representations.

anchor.quote: negotiates with, contests, and subverts Euro-American ideologies and representations

facts.text: Language and literature helped consolidate national identity against colonial impact.

anchor.quote: Language and literature were factors in consolidating this sense of national identity

misconceptions.text: Students read postcolonial literature as writing that simply describes life after independence.
misconceptions.corrective: The category is defined by its argument, not its date: the writing contests the representations empire produced, which is why the coloniser's language and canon are themselves contested ground.

examples.text: A novelist writing in the coloniser's language to retell a history that colonial texts had told for them is contesting representation, not merely narrating it.

mcBank.stem: A novelist from a formerly colonised country writes in the coloniser's language in order to answer how colonial texts had represented their people. This is best read as
options: contesting colonial representation
evidence that the colonial canon was accepted
a frame narrative technique
magic realism by definition

definition.text: Literary translation is the mediation that carries a work across languages, and it is the condition under which most world literature is read.

anchor.quote: gain meaning through translation

facts.text: Works that succeed as world literature can gain meaning through translation, not merely survive it.

anchor.quote: Works that thrive as world literature are ones that work well and even gain meaning through translation

facts.text: Circulation beyond a work's linguistic point of origin is what carries it into world literature.

anchor.quote: circulating out into a broader world beyond its linguistic and cultural point of origin

misconceptions.text: Students treat a translation as a lossy copy whose gaps are always failures.
misconceptions.corrective: Translation is a reading as well as a transfer: a work can gain meaning in a new language, so the question is what a given translation makes available rather than only what it loses.

examples.text: Two translations of the same poem foreground different images, and comparing them shows what each translator judged to be the poem's centre.

mcBank.stem: Two translations of one poem differ in which images they foreground. The most defensible comparative claim a student can make is
options: each translation encodes a reading of the poem
the older translation is the accurate one
the poem is untranslatable
translation removes meaning in every case
